questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 29,4 m·s⁻¹. Taking upward as positive, calculate the time to reach maximum height, the maximum height, and the velocity with which it returns to the thrower's hand. State the ball's acceleration at the highest point.
questions.expected_answer: Take upward as positive, so a = −9,8 m·s⁻². At the top vf = 0. Using vf = vi + at: 0 = 29,4 − 9,8t, so t = 3 s. Maximum height from vf² = vi² + 2aΔy: 0 = 29,4² − 2 × 9,8 × Δy, so Δy = 864,36 ÷ 19,6 = 44,1 m. By symmetry the downward trip mirrors the upward one: the ball returns to the hand after a further 3 s (total flight 6 s) moving at 29,4 m·s⁻¹ downward — the same speed it left with, in the opposite direction. At the highest point the velocity is zero but the acceleration is still 9,8 m·s⁻² downward, because the gravitational force acts throughout the flight; the ball is momentarily at rest yet still accelerating.

questions.question: Sketch and describe the position-time, velocity-time and acceleration-time graphs for a ball thrown vertically upward at 29,4 m·s⁻¹ and caught at the same height, taking upward as positive. Explain how the three graphs are connected through gradients.
questions.expected_answer: Position-time: a parabola starting at zero, rising with decreasing steepness to a maximum at 3 s (half the flight), then falling with increasing steepness back to zero at 6 s; it records height against time, not the ball's path. Velocity-time: a straight line starting at +29,4, with constant gradient −9,8, crossing zero at 3 s — the moment of maximum height — and reaching −29,4 at the catch. Acceleration-time: a horizontal line at −9,8 m·s⁻² for the whole flight. The connections: the gradient of the position-time graph at any instant equals the velocity at that instant — steep at launch, zero at the summit (horizontal tangent), steep and negative at the catch — which is why the position graph must curve, since the velocity changes continuously. The gradient of the velocity-time graph equals the acceleration; because the line is straight, that gradient is the constant −9,8, which is exactly the flat acceleration graph. The area between the velocity-time graph and the time axis gives displacement: two equal triangles of 44,1 m each, one positive and one negative, summing to zero for a ball caught at its launch height, while the distance is 88,2 m.

questions.question: A ball is dropped, bounces twice, and is caught. With downward taken as positive, describe its velocity-time graph in detail, and explain why each straight segment has the same gradient while each bounce peak is smaller than the last.
questions.expected_answer: The graph starts at zero and rises as a straight line with gradient +9,8 as the falling ball gains speed, reaching its maximum positive value at the first floor strike. During the brief contact the graph plunges almost vertically from that positive value to a smaller negative value: the velocity reverses direction (the ball now moves upward, negative in this convention) and shrinks in magnitude because kinetic energy is transferred to sound, heat and deformation during the bounce. The line then rises again with the same gradient +9,8, crossing the time axis at the top of the bounce — the ball momentarily at rest in mid-air — and continuing positive as the ball falls once more, producing a sawtooth of parallel straight segments in which each tooth is shorter than the one before. The segments are parallel because between floor contacts the ball is a projectile: gravity is the only force acting, so the acceleration is always 9,8 m·s⁻² downward, and every segment must carry that same gradient. The peaks shrink because each bounce is inelastic — the ball leaves the floor slower than it arrived — so every new flight begins with less speed and reaches a lower height than the previous one.
